title: Objectives written into contracts, and whether any result is published
question: For the nonprofits paid most, what did their contracts say they must achieve, and has anyone published whether they did?
finding: The contracts and grant appendices on file for all of the 40 most-paid nonprofits list 2,836 distinct objectives, 1,283 of them with a percentage target. For 16 of those organizations, paid $431.0 million in fiscal year 2026 (a sum that includes money passing through them to others), no result naming them was found in the commission papers, monitoring tables or federal counts on disk. For the other 24 a summary exists (a monitor's score, a share of objectives met, a sentence, or beds occupied on the federal count night) but never the figure achieved against each objective. Of 108 homelessness contract memos that carry both the objectives and a performance history, 17 say whether objectives were met.
how: Objectives come from a table built by the download step from 400 documents: Board of Supervisors contract attachments, homelessness and human-services commission packets, and Public Health's objectives documents. Rows naming one organization are de-duplicated by their opening words; unit-of-service lines and boilerplate are dropped. A further 1,279 Public Health objectives apply system-wide to every contractor of a given type and are not counted against any one organization. The recorded result is the latest entry for that organization in the monitoring screen above. City money is taken from the Controller's table of every payment, less the payments it labels as loans, not from its narrower nonprofit-spending table, which keeps contracted services only. That figure includes money passing through: subsidies and insurance premiums that an organization pays on to others, and assessments that the City collects for a district and hands over. These are real City payments but not payment for the organization's own work. The fiscal year is the one printed on each payment, which can be later than the year the payment was made.
limits: The objectives were extracted mechanically: some rows are headings or fragments, the organization is sometimes inferred from the nearest name on the page, and the same objective can recur in an amendment with slightly different wording, so the counts are approximate; check the cited page. Departments collect results against these objectives in their own systems; what is missing is publication, not necessarily measurement. Public Health-only organizations show few objectives because their contracts point to the system-wide documents.

columns.t: One outcome objective, as written (cut at 25 words)
